porrum, i, n., and porrus, i, m.
πράσον
,
a leek, scallion; of two kinds, capitatum and sectile, the latter our chives, ; ; ; ; ; ; .

la:noun:porro.html:
porro, adv.
root pra-; Sanscr. prathamus, primus; Lat. prae, pro, prior; cf. Gr. πόρρω, πρόσω
,
forward, onward, farther on, to a distance, at a distance, after off, far.
Lit., in space, with verbs both of motion and of rest (rare and mostly anteclass.), : porro agere armentum,: ire,.—So ellipt.: porro Quirites, on! hither! ye Romans! Laber. ap. ; (al. proh).—With verbs of rest: habitare,: inscius Aeneas, quae sint ea flumina porro,: campi deinde porro,.—
Transf.
In time.
Of old, aforetime, formerly (very rare): altera (Nympha), quod porro fuerat, cecinisse putatur,.—
Henceforth, hereafter, afterwards, in future: me sollicitum habitum esse atque porro fore, Cato ap. P.; : quid in animo Celtiberi haberent aut porro habituri essent,: fac, eadem ut sis porro,; : move ocius te, ut, quid agam, porro intellegas,: dehinc ut quiescant porro moneo, prol. 22: hinc maxima porro Accepit Roma, et patrium servavit honorem,in aftertimes,.—
In a series.
In gen., again, in turn, : saepe audivi a majoribus natu, qui se porro pueros a senibus audisse dicebant,; .—
In partic., in discourse.
In the progress of an argument, or in a sequence of ideas, then, next, furthermore, moreover, besides: sequitur porro, nihil deos ignorare,; ; : age porro, tu, qui, etc.,; : Habonium porro intellegebat rem totam esse patefacturum,; ; : porro autem anxius erat, quid facto opus esset,: quid fit deinde? porro loquere,say on,: porro dicere,.—
Then, on the other hand, but: porro erant qui censerent,: porro si in digito Dei eicio daemonas, (but the true read., , is paene).

senses: of or pertaining to the gens Porcia.
la:adj:Porcius.html:
Porcius, i, m.; Porcia, ae, f.,
the name of a Roman gens. The most celebrated are,
M. Porcius Cato Censorinus, or Major, the severe censor, whose life was written by Nepos, and for whom Cicero named his Essay on Old Age, sqq.; .—
M. Porcius Cato, the younger, called Uticensis, because of his famous death at Utica, ; .—
In fem., Porcia, a sister of the younger Cato, wife of Domitius Ahenobarbus, ; .—Hence,
Porcĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Porcius, Porcian: lex, of the people's tribune P. Porcius Laeca, ; ; ; : basilica,named after the elder Cato,.

la:verb:porto.html:
porto, āvi, ātum, v. freq. a.
root porfor for-to, kindr. with fer-o; Sanscr. vhri, ferre
,
to bear or carry along; to convey any thing heavy (class.; syn.: fero, gero, veho).
Lit.: ferri proprie dicimus, quae quis suo corpore bajulat, portari ea, quae quis in jumento secum ducit, agi ea, quae animalia sunt, (the foll. pass. prove that this distinction is not valid): ut id, quod agri efferant sui, quascumque velint in terras portare possint,: hominem ad Baias octophoro,: Massili portabant juvenes ad litora tanas, Enn. ap. Don. p. 1777 P. (Ann. v. 605 Vahl.): frumentum,: viaticum ad hostem,; cf. : Massilium in triumpho,to conduct,: frumentum secum,: corpora insueta ad onera portanda,: panem umeris,: sub alā Fasciculum librorum,: aliquid in suo sinu,: ad modum aliquid portantium,: venter qui te portavit,: telum, hominis occidendi causā portare, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 1, 13, 1.—Esp. of ships, etc.: navis portat milites,: naves onerariae commeatum ab Ostiā in Hispaniam ad exercitum portantes,: commeatum exercitui,; —
Trop.
To bear, carry, bring (mostly poet.; not in Cic.): onustum pectus porto laetitiā,: alicui tantum boni,; cf.: di boni, boni quid porto!: porto hoc jurgium Ad uxorem,: alicui aliquam fallaciam,: timores insolitos alicui,: preces alicujus alicui,.—With abstract subjects: nescio quid peccati portet haec purgatio,bears with it, imports, betokens,: portantia verba salutem,bringing,: tristitiam Tradam protervis in mare Portare ventis,: salutem,.—In prose: sociis atque amicis auxilia portabant,: divitias, decus, gloriam, libertatem atque patriam in dexteris portare,: has spes cogitationesque secum portantes,: ad conjuges liberosque laetum nuntium portabant,: hic vobis bellum et pacem portamus,.—
To endure, bear, suffer (late Lat.): dolores nostros ipse portavit,; : judicium,.

la:noun:portus.html:
portus, ūs (
gen. sing. porti, Turp. ap. : dat. plur. portibus, et saep.; a better form than portubus), m.
por, whence porto, portitor
.—Prop., an entrance; hence,
A harbor, haven, port: Lunai portus, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 16 Vahl.): portus Caietae,; ; cf.: in Graeciae portus,: e portu solvere,to sail out of port,; so, e portu proficisci,: ex portu exire,: ex portu naves educere,; 2, 22: portum linquere,: petere,to sail into, to enter,; : capere,: occupare,: in portum venire,to enter the port,; so, in portum ex alto invehi,: in portum deferri,: in portum pervenire,: in portum se recipere,: in portum navim cogere (al. conicere),: in portum penetrare,: portum tenere,to reach a port,: in portum voluntatis deduci,: in portu operam dare,to be an officer of the customs,; .—With reference to the import-duty to be paid in ports: ex portu vectigal conservare,; . —Prov.: in portu navigare,i. e. to be in safety, out of all danger,; so, in portu esse,.—
Poet., transf., the mouth of a river, where it empties into the sea, ; .—
Trop., as also the Greek λιμήν, and our haven, a place of refuge, an asylum, retreat (class.; a favorite trope of Cicero): portus corporis, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 415 Vahl.): tamquam portum aliquem exspecto illam solitudinem,; so with tamquam,: se in philosophiae portum conferre,: regum, populorum, nationum portus erat et refugium senatus,: exsilium non supplicium est, sed perfugium portusque supplicii,; : hic portus, haec arx, haec ara sociorum,; so, nam mihi parta quies, omnisque in limine portus,i. e. security is at hand,: venias portus et ara tuis,: vos eritis nostrae portus et ara fugae,. —
In the oldest Latinity, a house (as a place which one enters): portum in XII. pro domo positum omnes fere consentiunt, Müll.—*
A warehouse: portus appellatus est conclusus locus, quo importantur merces et inde exportantur,: Licini,.

la:noun:porticus.html:
portĭcus, ūs, f. (also heteroclit.
acc. plur. PORTICOS, ) [porta], a walk covered by a roof supported on columns, a colonnade, piazza, arcade, gallery, porch, portico, = στοά.
Lit.: omnes porticus commetiri,: porticum aedificare,; : inambulare in porticu,: viae latae, porticus, etc.,: porticuum laxitas,: porticuum,; : in amplis porticibus,; cf. : me porticus excepit,; : porticus, in quā gestetur dominus,: triplex,.—In the upper story, .—
Transf. *
The entrance or porch of a tent (poet.): saucii opplent porticus, the porches, Att. ap. .—
A weather-board, shed, § 2; 9, 7, 4; 9, 14, 14.—
A long shed or gallery to protect soldiers in sieges, .—
The Porch or Portico, meaning the school of the Stoics (from στοά, porch, the place where Zeno taught); hence, transf., the Stoic philosophy, the Stoics: Chrysippus, qui fulcire putatur porticum Stoicorum,; cf. : clamat Zeno et tota illa porticus tumultuatur, ap. Aug. contr. Ac. 3, 7; .

la:noun:porta.html:
porta, ae (portabus for portis, Cn. Gell. ap. P.), f.
from root par-, to pierce, pass through; Gr. περάω, πείρω, πόρος, ford; Lat.: peritus, ex-perior, and v. periculum
,
a city-gate, a gate.
Lit.: hic (miles) portas frangit, at ille (amans) fores,: rectā portā invadam extemplo in oppidum antiquom et vetus,; : si Hannibal ad portas venisset,: pedem portā efferre,; ; : ad portam praesto esse,: portā introire,: egressus portā Capenā,: extra portam Collinam,: porta Carmentalis,: pars egressa portis erat,; : omnibus portis effundi,: portā Capenā Romam ingressus,; : signa portis efferre,: portis ruere,: eādem portā signa infesta urbi inferre,: patefactā portā Romani erumpunt,: subito omnibus portis eruptione factā,; ; : omnibus portis prorumpunt,; : portarum claustra,: limina portarum,: portas obice firmā claudere,: portas reserare hosti,: portā triumphali ducere funus,: sanctae quoque res, veluti muri et portae, quodammodo divini juris sunt,: vidi Portas (Carthaginis) non clausas, a proof that the people were fearless,.—Connected with urbis: qui urbis portas occuparent,: bellum a portis hujus urbis avolsum,.—With per (rare except in Livy): per unam portam praesidium Romanum irrumpit,: paulo ante lucem per effractam portam urbem ingreditur,: per aversam portam silentio excedere,; ; : elapsus per eam portam quae ... ad Darii castra pervenit,; : in fastigio portae,.—Prov.: porta itineri longissima, the way to the gate is the longest (sc. in making a journey), i. e. it is the first step that costs, .—
Transf., in gen., like our gate, of an avenue, entrance, passage, outlet, door of any kind (syn.: fores, janua, ostium). —Of the gates of a camp: ab decumanā portā castra munita,; so, principalis,: quaestoria,: villarum,: venti, velut agmine facto, Quā data porta, ruunt,

.—Of a cage: ex portā ludis emitti, said of hares,: porta tonat caeli, Enn. ap. Vet. Gram. ap. Col. (Ann. v. 597 Vahl.); : somni,; cf. eburna,: ubi portitor aera recepit, Obserat umbrosos lurida porta rogos,the portal of the infernal regions, belli portae, Enn. ap. ; (Ann. v. 271 Vahl.): mortis,: inferi,: portae, quae alibi Armeniae, alibi Caspiae, alibi Ciliciae vocantur,passes, gorges, defiles,; ; : solis,the signs of Cancer and Aries in the zodiac,, and S. 1, 17: jecoris, a part of the liver (so too in Gr. πύλη), : fluviorum,.—Of the fundament, .—*

Trop.
Et quibus e portis occurri cuique deceret, by what way, by what means, .—
As the symbol of strength: portae inferi,the powers of hell,.

la:verb:portendo.html:
portendo, di, tum, 3 (
inf. pres. portendier, ), v. a.
an archaic collat. form in relig. lang. of protendo, to stretch forth
, to point out, indicate (future events, misfortunes, etc.), to foretell, predict, presage, portend (cf.: ostendo, monstro): ea (auspicia) illis exeuntibus in aciem portendisse deos,; cf.: di immortales mihi sacrificanti ... laeta omnia prosperaque portendere,: magnitudinem imperii portendens prodigium,: populo commutationem rerum portendit fore, Att. ap. : triginta annos Cyrum regnaturum esse portendi,: quod portentum regni ruinam portendebat, of an earthquake,.—Pass., to be indicated (by a sign), to threaten, impend.
Usually of bad fortune, loss, injury, etc.: nobis periculum magnum portenditur,: haruspices dudum dicebant mihi, malum damnumque maximum portendier,; cf.: malum quod in quiete tibi portentum est,: quod in extis nostris portentum est,.—
Of good fortune, etc.: salvos sum: libertas portenditur,: quid spei Latinis portendi?. —Hence, portentum, i, n., a sign, token, omen, portent (syn.: ostentum, prodigium).
Lit.: ex quo illa ostenta, monstra, portenta, prodigia dicuntur,; cf. Müll.; and Paul. ex Müll.: nam si quod raro fit, id portentum putandum est, sapientem esse portentum est,: portentum inusitatum conflatum est recens, Poët. ap. : alii portenta atque prodigia nunciabant,: ne quaere profecto, Quem casum portenta ferant,.—Of miracles, ; ; cf. .—
Transf.
A monster, monstrosity: cetera de genere hoc quae sunt portenta perempta,; : quale portentum neque militaris Daunias latis alit aesculetis Nec, etc.,: quae virgineo portenta sub inguine latrant,i. e. the dogs of Scylla,: praeter naturam hominum pecudumque portentis,monstrous births, monsters,; cf.: bovem quendam putari deum, multaque alia portenta apud eosdem, .—Trop., in a moral sense, a monster of depravity: P. Clodius, fatale portentum prodigiumque rei publicae,: Gabinius et Piso, duo rei publicae portenta ac paene funera,: qualia demens Aegyptus portenta colat,.—
A marvellous or extravagant fiction, a strange tale, a wonderful story: cetera de genere hoc monstra et portenta locuntur,: poëtarum et pictorum portenta,: portentum atque monstrum certissimum est, esse aliquem humanā specie et figurā, qui tantum immanitate bestias vicerit,: portenta atque praestigias scribere,.

la:noun:portorium.html:
portōrĭum (
dat. plur. PORTORIEIS, Plebisc. Thermens ap. Orell. 3673), ĭi, n.
root por, whence porto, portitor, portus, that belongs to carrying or conveying; hence
,
A tax, toll, duty, impost paid on goods imported or exported: portorium dare, Lucil. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Caecil. ap. ; ; cf.: ego pol istum portitorem privabo portorio,: portorium circumvectionis,a tax paid for the right of hawking goods about the country, a peddler's tax,.— *
Fare, freight, = naulum: Charon expetens portorium,.

la:noun:portitor.html:
portĭtor, ōris, m.
portus
,
a tollgatherer (at a seaport), a receiver or collector of customs, a custom-house officer (syn. telonarius), ; ; ; ; (); they forwarded letters: epistulam ... ad portitores esse delatam,; cf.: portitorum simillimae sunt januae lenoniae; Si adfers, tum patent,.—On account of their strict examinations, transf., a woman who pries into every thing, .

la:verb:porricio.html:
porrĭcĭo (porĭ-), ēci, ectum, 3, v. a.
old prep. port (v. pōno) and root ric-, to extend; cf. rica, a flowing veil
.
Lit., to lay before, to offer sacrifice to the gods: exta porriciunto, diis danto in altaria, Veran. ap. : atrocia porriciunt exta ministratores, Naev. ap. ; : cruda exta in mare porricit,; cf.: extaque salsos Porriciam in fluctus, and 776; Fenest. ap. .—Prov.: inter caesa et porrecta ut aiunt, between the slaying and the offering of the victim, i. e. at the last moment, at the eleventh hour, .—*
Transf., apart from relig. lang., to bring forth, produce any thing: seges frumentum porricit,

la:other:Portunus.html:
Portūnus (less correctly Portum-nus), i, m.
portus
,
the protecting god of harbors, also called Palaemon, ; ; Serv.; ; ; Paul. ex .—Hence,
Portūnālis (Portumn-), e, adj., of or belonging to Portunus, Portunal: flamen, Poët. ap. Fest. s. v. persillum, p. 217 Müll.—
Subst.: Portūnālĭa, ĭum, n., the festival of Portunus, celebrated annually on the 17th of August, Müll.; Calend. ap. .

la:verb:porrigo.html:
porrĭgo, rexi, rectum, 3 (contr. form porgo, porgite, Enn. ap. , and :
porge,; : porgebat, Sil 9, 458: porgens,: porgi,: porxit,; cf.: antiqui etiam porgam dixerunt pro porrigam, Müll.—Acc. to Lachmann, , instead of perditur, we should read porgitur; v. perdo init.), v. a.
por, = pro, and rego
, to stretch or spread out before one's self, to put forth, reach out, extend (class.; syn. extendo).
Lit.
In gen.: jam dudum, si des, porrexi manum,. 7, 49: animal membra porrigit, contrahit,: manum ad tradendam pyxidem,: crus,: caelo bracchia,: aciem latius,.— Pass., to stretch or spread one's self out, to be stretched out, extended: (Tityos) per tota novem cui jugera corpus Porrigitur,extends,. 596: porrectus somno,: serpens in longam porrigi alvum,; cf.: serpens centum porrectus in ulnas,; Trogus ap. .—So freq. of localities, to stretch out, extend, to lie (mostly post-Aug.): cubiculum porrigitur in solem,: cujus (loci) pars colles erant, pars in planitiem porrigebatur,: Creta inter ortum occasumque porrigitur,; . —
In partic.
To lay at full length, to stretch on the ground (rare): in plenos resolutum carmine somnos, Exanimi similem, stratis porrexit in herbis,: utrumque ab equis ingenti porrigit arvo,: in spatium ingens ruentem porrexit hostem,; .—
To hold forth, reach out, to offer, present: dexteram alicui,: dextram,: bona alicui,; cf.: munera,: pocula,: gladium alicui ad occidendum hominem,; : manum sani medicis porrigunt, .—Prov.: maritali porrigere ora capistro,to present his head to the marriage halter,.—
Porrigere manum, in voting, to put forth or hold up the hand, .—Hence, transf., i. q. to express one's assent or approval: quare si tu quoque huic sententiae manum porrigis,.—
Trop.
To protract, prolong (syn. prolato): iter,; ; so of the quantity of a syllable: syllabam,; cf.: ut aliquis impetum morbi trahendo effugiat, porrigaturque in id tempus, etc.,i. e. be kept alive, supported,.—
(Acc. to I. B. 2.) To offer, to grant a thing: praesidium clientibus porrigere atque tendere,: et mihi forsan, tibi quod negarit, Porriget hora,.—
Manus ad (in) aliquid porrigere, to reach after, strive for, seek to obtain (mostly post-Aug.): Lydiam cepisti ... jam etiam ad pecora nostra avaras et insatiabiles manus porrigis,: fames me appellat, ad proxima quaeque porrigatur manus,; ; ; ; : manus suas in orientem occidentemque porrexit,; cf.: pecunia deesse coepit, neque quo manus porrigeret suppetebat, nisi, etc.,.—
Se porrigere, to extend, reach, spread itself: jam fortuna Romana se ad orientalia regna porrigere coeperat,: quis gradus ulterior, quo se tua porrigat ira, restat?.—porrectus, a, um, P. a., stretched out, extended, long.
Lit.: porrecta ac aperta loca,: locus,: syllaba,long,; cf. mora,long, protracted,: senex, stretched out, i. e. dead, ; cf. in double sense: tuam amicam video. Ca. Ubi ea'st? Ps. Eccam in tabellis porrectam, .—Comp.: porrectior acies,: porrectior frons, i. e. more cheerful (opp. contractior), .—
Subst.: porrectum, i, n.
Extent: Thessaliae in porrectum longitudo,. —
A straight line, .—
A plain, .—Plur., . —
Trop., widespread, extended: famaque et imperī Porrecta majestas ad ortum Solis ab Hesperio cubili,.— Hence, adv.: porrectē, widely, extensively, far (post-class.).—Comp.: porrectius ire,farther,; .

Lit.: Luna aequā portione divisa,: ex his portio in Italiā consedit, portio in Illyricos sinus penetravit, : hereditatis,; cf. : quamvis quota portio faecis Achaei,: mox in proflatum additur tertia portio aeris collectanei,: pari portione inter se mixta pix, cera, alumen, etc.,; cf.: glandis cortex et nitrum paribus portionibus,: nil natura portionibus parit,by parts, piecemeal,: portio brevissima vitae,: pars A carnaniae, quam in portionem belli acceperat,as his share for his services in the war,: vocare aliquem in portionem muneris,: magna mortalium portio,.—
Transf., a relation to any thing, proportion, i. q. proportio.—
In gen., adverb.
prō portiōne (class.; not in Cæs.), in proportion, proportionally, relatively: pro portione ea omnia facito,: pro portione ad majorem fundum vel minorem addere,: Mamertinis pro portione imperaretur,; ; : oportet ut aedibus ac templis vestibula et aditus, sic causis principia pro portione rerum praeponere,in relation, in proportion,; so, pro ratā portione,: pro suā scilicet portione,; .—
